response_text: The concept of round-robin scheduling involves allowing an ordered list of tasks to run in a rotating order for a short, but equal amount of time. At the end of this time, if a task has not completed, it is paused, sent to the back of the list, and the next task begins to run. This process can be implemented with a queue, which uses the heap to address each task dynamically in memory (using pointers) to enqueue and dequeue tasks as they run in a rotating schedule. Scheduling with an array (static memory), however, requires manual indexing and shifting of task positions in a list, which can be a more complex process in terms of processing time, allocated memory, and code needed for implementation. Using a queue for a rotating schedule of tasks is more beneficial in this case as it allows for flexible queue sizes and more straightforward written implementation.\n
